The Mottled piculet (Picumnus nebulosus) is a small Neotropical woodpecker whose reproductive biology has been relatively little studied compared to other picids. Available data indicate that adult females attain an asymptotic body mass of 11.8 grams [Wwi = 11.8 grams], a value consistent with the diminutive size characteristic of the genus. The initial egg mass, measured just prior to hatching and assumed to represent the wet weight at birth, has been recorded at 1.4 grams [Wwb = 1.4 grams], reflecting the substantial energetic investment required to produce a fully formed calcareous egg relative to the mother's small frame. This species is reported to lay a single clutch per breeding season, with clutch sizes ranging from 1 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 4 eggs per clutch]. The annual reproductive frequency is limited to approximately 1 clutch each year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch each year], a pattern typical of many tropical and subtropical woodpeckers that face relatively stable but resource-limited environments.

Incubation in the Mottled piculet proceeds under tightly regulated thermal conditions, with eggs maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] throughout the developmental period. The incubation interval, representing the age at hatching from the onset of consistent brooding, has been documented to last 17 days [ab = 17 days], a relatively brief duration that aligns with the rapid development expected for a bird of such low absolute body mass at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Upon emergence, the altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning and brooding for thermoregulation. The critical stage of fledging, when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and begins to leave the nest cavity, occurs at 23.5 days after hatching [tx = 23.5 days after hatching] under typical thermal conditions of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] for active metabolic periods. This developmental timeline places the species on the faster end of the spectrum among woodpeckers of comparable size.

Following the fledging stage, the young Mottled piculet enters a period of continued growth and refinement of foraging skills while still occasionally soliciting food from its parents. Reproductive maturation proceeds over a significantly longer timeframe. The onset of puberty, marked by the development of functional gonads and the associated hormonal changes necessary for breeding, occurs at 70.5 days after hatching [tp = 70.5 days after hatching] when metabolic activity is supported by a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity is somewhat faster than what is observed in larger-bodied picids, such as the pileated woodpecker Dryocopus pileatus, and likely reflects a life-history strategy emphasizing early reproduction to compensate for comparatively modest clutch sizes. The species thus appears to allocate resources toward reaching reproductive competence within roughly two and a half months of leaving the nest cavity.

The interval between hatching and the initiation of a first successful nesting attempt is considerably more protracted than the time to gonadal maturation alone. Based on available observations, first-time breeders typically begin their initial brood at approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching], with this developmental milestone occurring under the same thermal regime of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] that characterizes active metabolic states. This delay of roughly one full year between birth and first reproduction suggests that young birds require an extended period to establish territories, acquire sufficient foraging proficiency, and accumulate the energetic reserves necessary to support egg production and incubation. The gap between reaching puberty and actual breeding highlights the importance of non-physiological constraints—such as social competition and resource availability—in shaping the species' reproductive phenology.

Longevity records for the Mottled piculet are scarce, but estimates derived from closely related species within the family Picidae suggest a potential maximum lifespan of approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years] under field conditions that support active metabolism at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This figure, comparable to the known lifespan of the larger pileated woodpecker Dryocopus pileatus upon which the estimate is based, would represent a substantial reproductive window for a bird that begins breeding at one year of age. Across that potential lifespan, the combination of a modest clutch of 1 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 4 eggs per clutch] and a single annual reproductive event [F_R_i = single annual reproductive event] yields a moderate lifetime reproductive output. The species' conservative reproductive strategy, characterized by low clutch frequency and a delayed age at first reproduction, appears well suited to the stable but resource-limited environments of the Atlantic Forest where it is primarily distributed.
